headline: First person, a water cooler that spreads knowledge, foosball warnings, and a cash sparkline

items.title: First-person camera modes
items.body: See the office through a staff member's eyes, or walk around it on foot. See as, on a person's card, shows the office from their eyes. Walk, beside the camera turn buttons, lets you explore it yourself: on desktop with WASD or arrows and the mouse to look, on touch with a stick under your left thumb and a drag on the right half of the screen to look. Escape or Exit returns you to the normal view. In first person the windows show the real street outside instead of the painted backdrop.

media.caption: See as: the office through Nathan's eyes, with the Seeing as tag and Exit
Walk: on foot among the desks, with the Walking tag and the controls hint
A window pane in first person: left the painted backdrop, right the see-through glass

items.title: The water cooler brings knowledge sharing
items.body: The coffee corner is now a water cooler where people gather and share what they know. Each person with a desk in reach closes 2% of their gap to the most knowledgeable person in reach each week, up to 1 point, when two or more people with desks in reach of the cooler are in the office. The cooler looks its era: a glass jug with a spigot on a wooden stand in the pre-internet, a blue-bottle cooler with a cup cabinet in the dot-com and classic years, a filtered tap on reclaimed wood in Web 2.0, and a white hydration station from Agents on. Two people stop by with paper cups now and then, sip and chat, then head back to their desks, with the chatter turned out toward the room so you see their faces. The cooler glugs now and then, its shop icon is an upside-down bottle on a dispenser, and build mode shows the largest cooler share in reach of a desk, not the sum.

media.caption: The water cooler's models, one per era
Two people chat at the cooler, turned out toward the room

items.title: Back to title in Settings
items.body: Settings now has a Back to title button that shows when you're playing. Tap it and confirm to save your game and return to the title screen, where Continue picks your company back up. The confirm scrolls into view when it opens.

media.caption: Back to title in Settings, with its confirm: Save and go, or Stay

items.title: Cash sparkline in the HUD shows cash trends
items.body: The cash display now shows a small graph of the last 40 weeks of cash next to the number, except on phones and the Low quality setting. The line is green while cash has been climbing lately (it follows the last 6 weeks), amber when it falls or you have under 30 weeks of runway, and red when you have 12 weeks of runway or less, or are in the red and still losing money. A dashed line marks zero when cash has been below it. Tap the cash display to open the full money chart.

media.caption: Cash with its 40-week graph in the top bar

items.title: Foosball tables show when they can't play
items.body: A foosball table needs clear room on both long sides to work, and now the game tells you when one doesn't. While placing furniture, an amber preview warns if the new item would block a game or gets blocked. A placed table with no room gets an exclamation mark bubble over it, and the item card explains why the games stopped.

media.caption: An amber preview while placing, and an exclamation bubble over a table with no room
The build bar says "Needs room on both long sides"

items.title: Smaller fixes
items.body: Starting a product with automation on no longer requires picking a team. The Settings switches on phones now centre their knobs in the full height of the pill. Water cooler visits no longer clip through the cooler, and staff sipping hold their mugs properly. Printer carriers clear the printer without clipping through it when they carry it out back, and step onto their grips at walking pace. Mailed events pick their text from the era template, so the same mail arrives no matter what you named things. A Network Operations Center with chairs keeps two rows clear in front of it, for placement and upgrades. A letter that the queue presents gets a short ping. The post menu in Yak and DeskNet keeps its rows from overprinting each other and stays inside the Yak panel. The enterprise RFP binder shows POLICY on one spine and FINAL on the other.

headline: Fewer popups and an inbox, the era choice comes first, and the game installs for offline play

items.title: Fewer interruptions, more flow
items.body: The game now shows about 0.4 asks a running minute instead of constant popups. Most random events still happen, but only the biggest ones break in as cards. The rest play out quietly with a careful choice and post to Yak. Decisions, Yak prompts and letters wait in a queue and come one at a time, at least 90 seconds of running play apart (150 above 1x speed; emergencies skip the wait), and a prompt or letter you have seen closes after 120 seconds of running play. Status news (someone's back, running on empty, a project at 75%, a product shipping) shows as a small bubble in the office instead of a toast, so the team's mood reads in the room. A minor incident is a red bubble, the all-clear turns green. Company news floats as a gold banner. A new product gets one launch card and no launched toast, a small unlock gets a New pip and one toast instead of a card, the advisor button pulses three times when advice arrives and then glows, and Yak counts only incidents, wins and important posts as unread, with flavour posts at least 20 seconds apart. When an ask times out, its default is a careful choice that costs at most a little, such as a small counter-offer when a bigger company poaches someone.

media.caption: Status news as bubbles over the team: back, 75% done, a minor outage, running on empty, and a gold company banner

items.title: Office gags play out without a card
items.body: The office gags (ping-pong, the printer jam, the chewed cable, the trips to the expo and the AI summit) now resolve on their own. Their prop stays up for about 15 seconds of running play and a short caption bubble names what happened, such as "Printer jammed" or "Cable chewed". A desk bubble waits until the person it is over has finished speaking.

media.caption: The chewed cable gag plays out in the office with no card
Ping-pong: a bubble over a player and no card

items.title: The inbox is on
items.body: An envelope button in the top bar (or the I key) opens a Mail panel. Letters start arriving in week 4 and ask for an answer, about one every eight minutes: a recruiter after one of your people, the blockchain pitch, the app store rejection and, from week 26, a partnership offer. A letter that waits pings, and the envelope pulses three times and keeps a steady badge until you read it. An open letter reads on its own stationery card. A reply-all storm turns up as a Yak gag.

media.caption: The envelope in the top bar
A letter on its own stationery card in the Mail panel

items.title: The era choice comes first
items.body: New Game now opens on an Era step: all eight starts as cards, each with its share of Classic's score, Classic chosen, and Found a company or Take over a company below them. The Funding step names your pick and has a Change button back to it. The dice beside the company name draw from about 50 stock parody names, with a few for each starting era. Long company names now fit on the old logo sign at the alumni reunion and on the rival's sign.

media.caption: New Game opens on the Era step: the eight starts as cards, Classic chosen

items.title: Install it and play offline
items.body: The public build can be installed (Install app in Chrome, Add to Home Screen on iPhone and Android). Installed, it downloads the whole game in the background after the first launch, shows a progress pill and then "Ready to play offline", and plays offline in every era. A normal browser tab downloads nothing unless you tap Settings, Offline, Download. A newer release downloads in the background and asks "A new version is ready. Restart to update?". Settings also has a Full screen button, hidden where the browser has no full screen or the game is installed.

media.caption: Settings with the Full screen button

items.title: Boxed software asks for its first batch
items.body: After a boxed launch in the pre-internet, a card says boxed software sells from stock and offers 100 copies, 500 copies or Hold off, which points you at Reports > Inventory. When a product sells its last copy with buyers still asking and nothing on the way, a Sold out card offers the same reorder, once per sell-out.

media.caption: The Empty shelves card: 100 copies, 500 copies or Hold off

items.title: Decision props sit where you can see them
items.body: The props that decisions leave on a desk now go where the camera sees them best, instead of hidden behind a monitor. If every spot on the desk is hidden, a prop shrinks a little to fit. The policy binders are now one larger binder.

media.caption: Sticky notes on the desk
Mugs piling higher
One big POLICY binder on the desk

items.title: Smaller fixes
items.body: A decision card raised over the big Yak view can be answered; it used to sit underneath and freeze the game. Yak prompts whose cause stays true for months, like review code, buy a desk and take to lunch, stop coming up again and again. The deal handbell rings at most once every 30 seconds. People walk round furniture on their way to and from coffee, shelves and desk exits, and the printer carriers stand clear of the wall. The top bar fits on a 360 px phone with the envelope, and full-screen mode keeps the page filled, with its Back to full screen button kept off the toasts. A letter that was resolved while it waited behind a decision is skipped instead of coming up afterwards.

headline: Era starts for every new game, a droning all-hands screen for the open-plan decision, and faces, bells and props that read

items.title: Every new game can start in a different decade
items.body: Era starts are on for everyone now. The founding screen still defaults to a Classic 2019 company, but one tap on Change opens eight starts: pre-internet software in boxes, the dot-com boom, Web 2.0, Classic, the ChatGBT moment, Agents, Consolidation and the Plateau. The early starts carry on through the bust and Y2K. Each start dresses the office for its decade: CRT monitors and cubicles, a BOOM/BUST chart on the wall, a Y2K countdown clock, period clothes on the staff, and a street outside that changes from payphones and video-rental signs to parcel drones and a data centre going up next door. Some earlier starts score less than the full Classic career, so the long game stays the prestige run: a pre-internet start's score is multiplied by 0.67, dot-com by 0.61 and Web 2.0 by 0.56.

media.caption: A dot-com and a pre-internet start, next to Classic
Staff in period clothes
All 28 era objects

items.title: The open-plan decision goes through an all-hands screen
items.body: The open-plan decision still costs what it did. Knocking the walls down costs $2,000, gives Output +8% for 26 weeks and cuts Meaning recovery by 30% for the same 26 weeks. Keeping them changes nothing. What changed is the moment: it is now a parody of the famous 1984 ad. A wall screen shows a bald leader in dark glasses droning on about alignment, a rising sting plays as someone runs in, and the hammer goes through the screen with a shatter and static. The caption reads "The all-hands screen drones on about alignment. Someone has a hammer.", and the leader's lines join the usual talk.

items.title: The Banner Rotation Server finally looks like one
items.body: The Banner Rotation Server stopped being a tan crate: it now has a model at each of its three levels, starting with a beige tower and a CRT showing a banner ad under a striped web-banner sign. It is only available and effective during the dot-com era. Level 1 costs $3,000 and adds 5% dot-com customer acquisition, level 2 costs $6,000 for 10%, and level 3 costs $12,000 for 15%.

media.caption: The Banner Rotation Server

items.title: Faces that show how people feel
items.body: Characters now have real faces: brows, lids, eyes that look around, and a mouth that changes shape. Burnt-out staff get a hollow stare and rare blinks. Responders panic during an outage, then grit their teeth until the all-clear. A seller who closes a notable deal looks smug, new hires look delighted, and clicking someone makes them look up at you, turning their chair toward the camera when they can. Voice barks move the speaker's mouth with the audio and set their expression (delighted, one brow up for a question, side-eye when annoyed, heavy lids when tired). Portraits show the same face the person has in the office, and faces keep working while the game is paused.

items.title: Closing a big deal rings a bell
items.body: When a notable deal closes, the seller spins their chair toward you and rings a silver handbell beside their head, two quick shakes, under a sparkle for about 2.6 seconds while the two nearest seated coworkers turn and clap. It replaces the cash register sound, and the bell only plays when you can actually see it rung. The old fist pump never read from above: chibi arms can't reach past their own eyes.

items.title: Parties and music nights you can actually see
items.body: At a company party, seated staff now stand up behind their chairs and cheer with both arms in the air for 3 seconds, under a bigger banner that stays up through the cheer and wraps on a phone. At music night, a daily standup used to freeze everyone into a ring with their backs to the camera, hiding the dancer. Now the standup ends when the music starts, and up to four onlookers stand in an arc that leaves the dance in full view.

items.title: Moments are framed the same at every office size
items.body: At HQ, decision moments used to show far more floor than in the garage or on the Office Floor, so people were tiny. Moments now frame about the same number of metres at every stage, so the consultants and the hearing summons come in closer. The closest manual zoom scales with the office as well, so a bigger office goes in closer, and phones in portrait no longer get pushed to maximum zoom on every moment. The bridge loan's red screen now also pulses the room light red and puts a red vignette on the screen edges, even in a wide shot.

items.title: Decision props you can read
items.body: Six props that decisions leave behind were too small to make out, even zoomed all the way in. They're bigger and bolder now: a memo board covered in sticky notes, a leaning tower of mugs, three fat binders labelled POLICY, POLICY and FINAL, a fan of gift cards each with a big dollar sign, the old LOOPWORKS alumni sign at twice the size, and the mission-statement mug with its SOFTWEAR typo turned to face you. The chewed cable is thick hazard yellow with sparks at the bite. The closest zoom on the Office Floor goes in further too, from 3.2 to 5.

media.caption: All six at the closest zoom
SOFTWEAR, before and after

items.title: A summons and a coffee machine that read
items.body: The hearing summons is a fat red envelope with a gold seal, and its reader holds it up so you can see it. When the coffee machine dies, the fumes now rise from the espresso machine instead of an empty corner, and the smoke lingers while the staff fan it away.

items.title: People stop walking through the furniture
items.body: Staff used to cut corners, sometimes literally: heads brushing chair backs, a coffee run straight through a bookshelf, people standing inside the coffee counter. Walks now keep a step off furniture where there's room and go down the middle of corridors, standing spots keep a body's width clear, and people come at a seat from the side only when the slide onto it is clear. Contacts with furniture across a full test sweep fell from about 13,800 to 2,300.

items.title: Era cheers keep playing under a radio
items.body: The era-start cheer and the dot-com bust sting now fire when the era changes instead of when the music switches, so they still play when a different music track is already running.

items.title: Smaller fixes
items.body: Nobody facepalms while lying down any more, which used to spin people napping on the couch. The seated facepalm of the widest builds now lands on the eye. The Ops incident log header says "1 incident" and "1 breach" at exactly one instead of "1 breaches".

items.title: Pre-internet starts score a little lower
items.body: The pre-internet start was scoring about 8 percent above its intended share of a Classic run, so its score factor dropped from 0.72 to 0.67. It now lands at 0.955 of Classic against a target of 0.95, and the other seven starts were left alone. Its exit bar stays at 1.3 times Classic's.

items.title: Inbox and boombox built, not switched on
items.body: The in-game inbox (an envelope button, a Mail panel with Inbox, Spam and Done tabs) and the office boombox (a model, six radio stations and staff taste emotes) landed in the code but stay off for now, so nothing in a game changes yet.

items.title: New art, rendered clean
items.body: The new objects and looks from this day, each on its own with a plain background. Things that come in levels show all three side by side.

headline: Boxed-software pre-internet start, Consolidation and Plateau starts, company takeovers, and sales you can see

items.title: A pre-internet start: boxed software and DeskNet
items.body: A new founding option starts the company in the pre-internet era with boxed software. Choosing it adds $240K to your funding and gives you three garage desks. In Build you pick a boxed release, then order 100, 500 or 1,000 copies in Reports > Inventory. Copies cost $8 each to make and take two playable weeks to arrive. They sell for $250 each, minus the retailer's 30% share, and reviews below 6 send back one copy in twenty. Mailed patches cost $2 per installed copy. Installed copies slowly age out, one in 520 a week, so owners buy the next version and a product that has sold to its whole market sells again. It is deliberately harder to survive the dot-com bust from here: in the dev's test runs the balanced bot reached Web 2.0 in 181 of 200 games, against 185 from a two-founder dot-com start. DeskNet, a green terminal chat, replaces the usual chat. All of this is still behind the eras switch.

media.caption: The pre-internet office

items.title: Consolidation and Plateau starts, optional takeovers, the long career
items.body: Two more founding options: Consolidation and the Plateau, each a four-desk garage with that era's tools and extra funding ($390K and $540K). Their scores count for 28% and 19% of a Classic run. In ChatGBT and Agents you can instead take over a company the game already built, with a score worth 55% of a Classic run in ChatGBT and 30% in Agents. The pre-internet and Classic cards name their route (The Long Career or Classic Career), and a finished long career is titled "The Long Career, complete" on the anniversary screen. The market also stops growing after 2039, so a Plateau start no longer faces rivals and project sizes that keep inflating for decades.

media.caption: Consolidation office
Plateau office

items.title: Sales you can see and hear
items.body: Closed deals now show up. A week with a first sale for a product, or sales above the company's own recent pace, toasts the salesperson, the customer (a parody company name) and the product, and clicking it opens that product in Reports. The pace test compares against the trailing 26 weeks, so small and big companies both get beats instead of the big ones getting a flood. Smaller weeks leave a quiet "Sales: N new customers this week" line in the wins channel. Boxed sales read "Retail moved N copies". A notable deal rings a cash register, at most every 30 seconds.

items.title: Share your run
items.body: The end screen now shows a run card with the company name and logo, route or era, years survived, ending, final score and three highlight stats. "Save as image" downloads a PNG named for the company, and "Copy image" puts it on the clipboard. It is built in the browser and nothing is uploaded.

items.title: A street outside the modern-era office
items.body: Classic through Plateau get their own street: cyclists (delivery riders with insulated boxes in most eras), hire scooters on the pavement in Classic, ChatGBT and Agents, and a data centre where the default camera can see it on every stage. It changes with the era. Classic shows a hoarded plot with a COMING SOON board, ChatGBT a building site with crane lights that read at night, Agents and Consolidation a finished windowless data centre with parcel drones overhead, and Plateau a dark, ivy-grown one with fewer cars. The garage's neighbour houses also get roofs that sit on their walls instead of sinking into them.

items.title: Disk duplicator and retail display get real models
items.body: The two pre-internet shop items stop being crate stand-ins and get real models and their own icons. The Disk Duplicator costs $3K, $6K or $12K and cuts the cost of making each batch of copies by 10%, 20% or 30%. It goes from a beige drive tower to twin towers to a floor-standing autoloader beside a packing table. The Retail Display costs $2K, $4K or $8K and raises retail demand by 10%, 15% or 20%. It goes from a table of boxed software to a store endcap to a double endcap with a giant box standee.

media.caption: Disk duplicator

items.title: Goal order, touch sizes, card lettering and low-end speed
items.body: Goals list the current chapter first, so a dot-com start no longer opens on a later chapter's goal. Reports stop printing "null" in product subtitles, and the quiet chat banner names the office tab. Chat buttons are 40 px on touch and a scrolling tab row gets an edge fade. Card lettering no longer shows touching letters running together. On weak devices the Low setting renders at half resolution on software graphics and skips the extra full-screen passes, roughly three times faster on a 2-core software renderer.

items.title: New art, rendered clean
items.body: The new objects and looks from this day, each on its own with a plain background. Things that come in levels show all three side by side.

items.title: Nothing new to see
items.body: No player-facing changes landed today. Only dependency updates went in.

items.body: No player-facing changes landed today. The work went into checks and tooling behind the game.

headline: Era starts for the dot-com boom, Web 2.0, ChatGBT and Agents arrive behind a preview switch with their own decisions and exit bars, and game time keeps pace on slow machines

items.title: Found your company in a different era
items.body: Behind the ?eras preview switch, the founding screen now offers Classic, ChatGBT or Agents starts. Every start begins in the Garage with two founders and a full career of twenty modern years (the dot-com and Web 2.0 starts add their own years first). ChatGBT adds $90K and a third desk, and Agents adds $240K and four desks. Each era card shows its expected score as a share of Classic's, and each start's IPO and acquisition bars are scaled so it exits about as often as Classic: ChatGBT needs 0.8 times Classic's MRR and Agents 0.7 times. Agents also gets five years of milder incidents: severity is capped for its first 260 weeks. Without the switch, founding looks the same as before.

media.caption: ChatGBT start
Agents start

items.title: The dot-com boom and bust
items.body: With ?eras on, you can found a company in the dot-com years: two founders, four desks and $140K on top of your funding. Customer acquisition speeds up in week 26. In week 78 you can stay private for brand, or take a $180K public float that dilutes your score by 20% and costs you when the bust lands. A warning arrives in week 104, and in week 156 the bust hits. Preserving cash loses 25% of your live-product customers, while calling every customer loses 10% and costs the lesser of $20K and 10% of your cash. Public companies pay the lesser of $50K and 20% of cash first. In 1999, Build > Projects offers Y2K compliance contracts at 40 work points and $18K each, up to three, and Clive offers to cover New Year's Eve at triple rate for $9K, with no extra protection. At the rollover staff gather, count down, and one printer spits out an invoice dated 01/01/1900. At week 208 the company carries on into the Web 2.0 years, then Classic.

items.title: Web 2.0 and the browser years
items.body: A Web 2.0 start gives you three garage desks, $90K extra funding and the Internet Exploder 6 years. New web projects carry 20% extra compatibility work, or 8% with a senior Legacy Whisperer on the team, and you see the estimate before you start. Engineers earn credit only for launches they actually worked on, and three compatible launches qualify a senior engineer for the trait. Three decisions come up. Funding the QA bench costs $8K and cuts comprehension debt by 5. For the Active-ish control, a sandbox costs $5K and cuts comprehension debt by 2, an exception adds 5, and an ordinary form does nothing. Patching the grey PNG loader costs $1K and adds 3 polish to a compatible product. Your company carries over intact when the era hands off to Classic.

items.title: Market difficulty follows the calendar
items.body: In era careers, how hard the market is now follows the calendar, while company costs follow how old your company is. Rival clones, review expectations, project size, market size and the talent pool all track the year, so an era start meets the market of its own time and better hires arrive as the market gets harder. Incident bills, tenure, cooldowns and salaries stay on company age. In a Classic career the two clocks are the same, so nothing changes there.

items.title: Score factors and exit bars re-tuned
items.body: Each era start's score is now set so it lands below the Classic path: about 90% of Classic for dot-com, 75% for Web 2.0, 67% for ChatGBT and 40% for Agents. The IPO and acquisition MRR bars scale to match, at 1.35 times Classic's for dot-com, 1.2 for Web 2.0, 0.8 for ChatGBT and 0.7 for Agents. Saved companies keep the score factor they were founded with, and the Retire panel's IPO requirement now shows the scaled bar.

items.title: Game time keeps pace on slow machines
items.body: Game time now follows the wall clock at any frame rate, so a machine drawing fewer than four frames a second no longer plays fewer weeks than a fast one. Coming back to a hidden browser tab restarts the clock instead of replaying the time you were away.

items.title: Chat apps that look like their period
items.body: AwayIM gets square bevels, a blue title bar and an hourglass buddy icon, and HipCheck gets blue-grey rooms and presence status. Early messages use original period copy, and early posts forward jokes instead of picture memes. The pre-internet, dot-com and Web 2.0 eras also have their own emblems for the arrival card and HUD. The AwayIM away line now shows once in the status bar instead of also appearing as a teammate's post.

media.caption: AwayIM
HipCheck

items.title: Period music and sounds for the early eras
items.body: Pre-internet, dot-com and Web 2.0 each get two music loops, plus a subdued pair for the dot-com bust. Arriving in an era plays its own stinger, and the bust has one when the market turns. Chat apps ping in their own voice, and launches play a floppy seek, CD tray or retail box sound, with a bell when you take the small float.

items.title: Period offices, billboards and clothing
items.body: Era careers now look like their time. Offices get beige CRT desks, cubicle dividers, desk phones, dot-matrix printers, faxes, Rolodexes and a cork board with a wall calendar. Nine billboard jokes sit outside, including a giant OnlineLand floppy and the Parcel Paws sock-cat, and they switch from painted boards to LED ads as years pass. Staff wear period shirts, ties and vests with eight original parody tees, and each era hangs its own emblem on the office wall. A dot-com company started the old way, without picking an era, gets all of this too.

Pre-internet office

items.body: Staff stop walking through each other in narrow aisles, at crossings and past people standing still. Company parties no longer double up on slow machines, toasts and reveals keep the same timing when the browser stalls, and picking an era in the founding dialog no longer makes it fade out and restart.

headline: A Network Operations Center and an office robot to buy, a printer jam that now always happens, and advisor options that point at real actions

items.title: The Network Operations Center
items.body: A new Network Operations Center item helps you catch incidents early and end outages faster. It needs Ops and Security, you can have one per office, and upgrading needs a bigger office. Level 1 costs $8,000 and catches 8% more early and fixes outages 10% faster. Level 2 costs $30,000 for 15% and 20%. Level 3 costs $90,000 for 25% and 35%. It grows with the office through a TV on a cart, a dark room with a screen wall, and a full operations wall with a red beacon. Once the Agents era arrives and the NOC is level 2, a decision asks who watches it. Keep humans on the glass and it needs 3 people on security for the full effect, with no misreads. Let the agents watch and it catches about 1.5 times as much with no crew, but 15% of the time they misread a real alert and that incident lands one step worse. The Ops panel gets a card to switch modes, which is locked for a while after each change, with each mode's effect on its button and any refusal kept on screen.

media.caption: The NOC in the office
The NOC card in the Ops panel

items.title: The office robot rolls out
items.body: The Agents era gets a new item, the office robot, one per office. It costs $15,000, $45,000 or $120,000 for levels 1 to 3 and gives everyone a bit of stamina and meaning recovery: 8% and 3% at level 1, 12% and 5% at level 2, 16% and 7% at level 3. From level 2 it also waters a plant now and then. In the office it is a knee-high robot on a charging dock that brings coffee to a few people at their desks. It also breaks down in different ways: spinning by the coffee, nosing into an empty chair, holding a coffee beside an away person's desk, bumping a traffic cone, serving decaf under a storm cloud, or unplugged and slumped on its dock. Someone walks over and slaps it back to life. When it works, it serves at Waffle Parties and plays DJ at music night.

media.caption: The office robot

items.title: The printer lives in the kitchen
items.body: The printer jam moment is now guaranteed. It happens once in every game, between 8 and 48 weeks after you reach the Office Floor, instead of being a rare roll. Its three choices are unchanged: taking it out back costs $2,500 and gives the team +6 meaning, calling the repair line costs $300, and printing less cuts Output by 1% for 13 weeks and leaves a red OUT OF ORDER sign up for good. From the Office Floor on, the kitchen has a printer that shows READY, blinks, and hums through a print job now and then. It has no stats. The jam happens to that same printer, and afterwards the wreck, the repaired printer or the sign takes its place.

items.title: Advisor options point at a real action
items.body: Advisor suggestions now name a real action. Instead of "Pair someone with Eva on their work", it says "Put Vusi on Ledgerly v2 with Eva", and tapping it opens that person's card with the suggestion highlighted. You confirm before anything changes. Options can also highlight the Training or Time off button or open the Hire tab. A burnt-out person's card now offers Time off. Advice that had no matching control, like holding off on hiring, is gone. The advisor no longer suggests things you can't do.

items.title: Replies to your own Yak post show up
items.body: When you post on Yak, replies to your post are now shown first and no longer get dropped or expire behind other chatter. At the Important level, those replies also count as new on the collapsed Yak badge.

items.title: Facepalms, walking and a few small things
items.body: The Yak backfire facepalm now puts a palm over the eye the camera sees, both standing and seated. People no longer walk through each other, through plants and whiteboards, through NOC chair backs, through dancers at music night, or through the person still sipping at the coffee corner. People leaving the company walk round furniture placed in their way. The delete button for a save on the title screen stays armed for 10 seconds, or until you tap elsewhere, so a slower second tap deletes. A policy that only shows a toast no longer delays the next decision.

items.title: New art, rendered clean
items.body: The new objects and looks from this day, each on its own with a plain background. Things that come in levels show all three side by side.

media.caption: Office robot dock, three levels: the charging pad the coffee robot parks on.
The office robot: a coffee robot with a tray, a mug and a charging cable.
Pre-internet era: a beige CRT computer on a desk.
Pre-internet era: a cubicle wall.
Dot-com era: the Parcel Paws sock-puppet billboard across the street.

headline: Advisors with real options, tech debt that builds, squads, and incidents that explain themselves

items.title: Advisors who point out trouble
items.body: Three advisors (a CFO, a tech lead and a people lead) now notice what your panels already show and price the trade-off, but never give orders. The CFO speaks when you are under 12, 8 or 4 weeks of cash at your current burn. The tech lead speaks when tech debt hits 30, 50 or 70. The people lead speaks about burnout and unmentored juniors. Each piece of advice offers two or three things you could actually do, such as switching off Crunch Mode, starting The Big Refactor or putting someone on sales, and tapping one opens the right menu. A lightbulb in the top-right chip (shortcut H) opens their panel, with a red dot for a new notice and a portrait peek for the rare urgent one. A topic rests for 26 weeks after it speaks unless it gets worse.

items.title: Tech debt that builds and says why
items.body: Comprehension debt is now called tech debt everywhere, and it no longer sits at zero all game. It builds from project work, fastest with junior engineers, 1.5 times faster again under Crunch Mode, and it settles where paydown catches up, so it holds at a level instead of climbing without limit. Code Comprehension Reviews take 2.7% of the debt off each week, each senior engineer takes off a little more, and an engineer on maintenance takes off 0.2%. The Big Refactor now clears 60% of the debt instead of a flat 15. High debt hurts: security posture drops half a point per point of debt, rogue agents get more likely, and outages get harder to fix. The HUD meter shows last week's change and its tooltip breaks that down by source.

items.title: Squads
items.body: Once you have the Office Floor or 8 people, a Squads tab appears in Staff. A squad is a named group of 1 to 8 people with a lead, you can run up to 6, and you post one to a project as a unit. Squads that keep working together build cohesion over 12 weeks, worth up to 10% more output on their posting. Anyone joining or leaving halves it. After a squad ships a new product, its most knowledgeable engineers stay on as the upkeep crew and the rest sit out for two weeks, then go back to default work.

media.caption: The Squads tab in Staff

items.title: Incidents explain themselves
items.body: An outage now has a live card showing the cause in plain words, who is on it, how long until it is back, and the running cost in cash, brand and customers. Responders drop their project and maintenance work until the all-clear, so a bad outage costs you output too. If nobody can fix it, the card says so and offers Call for help. At the all-clear a summary lists what helped and what hurt, such as tech debt making the fix harder or having a blameless culture. For agent incidents the postmortem decision now comes at the end, with a choice to write it up properly or patch and move on. Responders stand round the server rack until the all-clear, then cheer.

items.title: Meeting table standups and desk rules
items.body: With a meeting table placed and Daily Standups on, the daily standup happens there, and everyone in it gains 0.3 knowledge. Async standups get nothing from the table. People sit round it and listeners turn to whoever is talking. New games start with a desk for each founder, at unchanged starting cash, and the first goal is now to make room for a hire with a third desk. A full office asks for a desk through Yak, and its choice opens desk placement. Promise one and add it within 4 weeks and the poster thanks you. Miss it and they lose 3 meaning. With no floor left, a new prompt nudges you toward a bigger office. Hiring with no free desk drops you straight into desk placement.

media.caption: Standup round the meeting table

items.title: Camera buttons, save files, and staffing shortcuts
items.body: Two HUD buttons turn the camera a quarter at a time, like Q and E. Saves can be exported as files and imported from the title screen, which also now says the game saves itself in this browser. Project cards get a Staff up button to move several people from maintenance or idle at once, filtered by role and level, and Automation lets you assign overseers inline. Opening a menu during a spotlight now lets the scene play on.

items.title: Styled memes
items.body: Yak gets memes drawn in the game's own style: Is this AGI?, a distracted founder, the bill, the plan, torn between two buttons, Change my mind with the printer, and a desk-lamp galaxy brain. Three of them (Is this AGI?, the distracted founder, the bill) show up once the ChatGBT era starts, and the plan waits for the Agents era. A Yak reply that opens something now opens it.

media.caption: Is this AGI?
Change my mind
Galaxy brain

items.title: Smaller fixes
items.body: Vacations are only postponed by an outage, Crunch Mode or a real push like founder hustle, and the toast names which. A banner on the wall no longer blocks them. Once the Incentives Program ladder is climbed, music night comes back every third award instead of every one. The first arcade level is now an actual arcade cabinet, and company parties show a banner saying what they celebrate. The desk squeeze prompt is about a full office blocking hires, not a missing desk. Moving an upgraded item previews it at its own level. The office move plays in view instead of behind the Office panel. Era carpets are quieter so team mats read, and ping pong players hold paddles.

items.title: New art, rendered clean
items.body: The new objects and looks from this day, each on its own with a plain background. Things that come in levels show all three side by side.

media.caption: Network operations centre, three levels: a TV on a cart, a curved console under a video wall, then a full ops room.

headline: Standups play whole conversations, pets stop clipping during greetings, and failed actions answer you during spotlights

items.title: Standups play whole conversations
items.body: Standups now play a complete five-line exchange in order, even when only two people are able to speak. Remote, absent and quiet colleagues stay out of the speaking parts. There are 21 short exchanges about projects, outages, oversight and ordinary work, with some memory so the same one doesn't repeat right away. If an outage clears mid-meeting, the conversation notices and moves on instead of still saying the product is down.

items.title: Pet greetings no longer clip
items.body: When someone stops to greet the office dog or cat, the pet now stays clear of the person while both turn. The pet takes a short step toward them, gets the full head scratch, then everyone goes back to walking. This also covers close spacing and pets arriving from odd angles.

items.title: Smaller fixes
items.body: A failed action now explains itself right away, even during a spotlight moment. Before, the reason waited until the moment ended. After a reload, Yak shows the posts you actually saw instead of bringing back the routine ones it had skipped. In the consultants scene, the person being interviewed now stands fidgeting with their head held still, so they read as facing the camera and the consultant at once.

headline: Six Silicon Valley decisions with real costs, no more back-to-back popups, and picture memes in Yak

items.title: The incubator house and The Box
items.body: Two new decisions, each coming up at most once a run. Early on in the garage (weeks 8 to 60), a would-be mentor offers free rent in his house for ten percent of the company. Moving in gives you $12K now and the final score gives up 10%, and a year later he shows up on a podcast calling himself your founder; keeping the garage costs nothing, and countering at five percent is a coin flip on getting the $12K. Once the Agents era is on and a rival is still going, The Box shows up: the rival's aluminium cube that does less for four times the price. Building your own costs $40K and adds some tech debt, but raises hype on your newest product and puts a little cube on a senior's desk for 26 weeks. Staying software gives a point of brand, and another when The Box is recalled 30 weeks later; mocking it is a gamble on brand.

items.title: Oat milk, kielbasa, tabs or spaces and squish
items.body: The other nods are smaller. Four thousand pounds of oat milk arrives when a procurement agent over-orders, but only in the first 26 weeks of the Agents era and only for a company with at least eight staff and 25% ops automation, so it stays uncommon. Send it back for $3,000, donate it for 2 brand, or keep it and everyone's stamina drains 10% slower for 52 weeks. Is it kielbasa? is a junior's app that is right half the time: ship it for 15 hype that fades by 8 six weeks later, sell the tech for $25K, or keep it as a demo for a boost to their meaning. Tabs or spaces is a running joke between two engineers in Yak that ends in a ruling, where each way to settle it costs the team a point of meaning. Squish is a new internal-tools research node (450 points, after CI/CD) that adds 5% reliability and slows health decay; when it ships, a #wins post cites a Squish Score nobody can explain.

media.caption: Oat milk decision

items.title: No two popups back to back
items.body: A new product launch or an unlock card now counts as a pausing moment, the same as a decision, so the game waits three weeks before raising the next decision. Random events that land inside that pause are held, up to two, and spent once the gap clears, so events do not thin out. Incidents and cyber attacks still interrupt right away. Version updates do not count, because that left decisions waiting too often.

items.title: Picture memes in Yak
items.body: Sharing a meme now posts an actual picture, drawn with the game's own people and office: This is fine, Two buttons, Tabs chart, Always config, Tests by the agent and Expanding review. Outages pick This is fine, and agent jokes wait for the Agents era. Tap a picture to enlarge it, and if the file is missing you get the caption as text.

media.caption: This is fine meme
Two buttons meme
Tabs chart meme

items.title: Calmer Yak and office chatter
items.body: Emoji reactions now scale with a post's weight: most chatter gets none or one or two, while wins, incidents, farewells and launches keep a full spread, with a rare pile of six to ten of one emoji as a joke. Office speech bubbles get a quiet beat between them. Queued Yak posts now expire after 30 seconds of game time at the current speed, so a stale outage line no longer shows after the outage is over.

items.title: Staged moments stay on topic
items.body: While a spotlight moment plays, the people in it and around it only say that moment's lines, so the crowd round a smashed printer no longer talks about launch posts. All 40 staged decisions and each of their choices have their own short dialogue, and the line after your choice reacts to what you picked. The letter, fumes and career milestone scenes now get the spotlight treatment too, with a caption and a tap-friendly Skip, and the waffle party and music night have captions. The sledgehammer is now held across both palms.

items.title: The office reacts to what happens
items.body: When a quick Yak post backfires, someone facepalms for about two seconds with their hand over their eyes, and nearby people turn to look with an exclamation or a sweat. When you place a new toy, the nearest free people (two for a pair table, one for anything else) walk over to try it a moment later, and keep looking for 20 seconds if nobody is free. Passing staff also stop to scratch an office dog or cat for three seconds before walking on.

media.caption: A Yak post backfires

items.title: Era carpets and a readable pivot board
items.body: Each era has its own carpet colour and pattern on the Office Floor and HQ annex: sand checks, teal ribbons, lilac squares, slate stripes and clay diamonds. The pivot whiteboard now faces the room and camera instead of showing its back, or goes up large on a back wall. The consultants' interview is staged a few metres in from the door so nobody walks through the shot.

items.title: Parody logos on press reviews, and a growth timeline that sticks
items.body: Launch reviews show four parody outlet logos: TechCrunchy, The Vergence, Hacker Olds and Wired-ish. The staff card's growth timeline now reads each person's saved history, so it survives a reload instead of restarting at Joined. On touch, the Place button dims while the aimed spot is blocked.

items.title: Smaller fixes
items.body: A desk scene such as the hearing summons now always seats someone who is actually in the office. If the named reader is away, the scene waits a week at a time, up to four weeks, then goes ahead at a present person's desk, so nothing queued behind it gets stuck. It also picks a new reader if theirs leaves that same week, and staged letters claim their named reader even if they are walking or in a standup.

headline: Late-game money sinks, far fewer pausing popups, founder replies in Yak, and a pile of office-movie decisions

items.title: Late-game money sinks: fame, a moonshot lab and the founders' last bet
items.body: Rich companies finally have something big to spend on. From the Consolidation era, once the office is big enough (the Office Floor), three fame campaigns open up in Marketing for a product or a new-product project: The Documentary ($400K or 6 weeks of revenue, whichever is more, for +20 fame), The Big Game Ad ($800K or 8 weeks, +25 fame and a burst of hype) and Stadium Naming Rights ($2M or 16 weeks, +35 fame, running 12 weeks). Fame fades 0.3 a week, and at 100 it cuts churn by up to 25% and hiring fees by up to 40%. About 100 weeks into Consolidation, with at least the Office Floor, a moonshot lab is pitched: funding it costs 25% of weekly revenue (at least $50K) every week, with a check-in every 26 weeks where you can keep going or pull the plug for a little fame. At the two-year mark it is unveiled, a 50/50 reveal (or you can give it six more months): a new product scoring 8.6 in a market you are not in yet, with +20 fame and +8 brand, or a glorious flop with +8 fame and -2 brand. At week 900 the founders get one last bet: one last moonshot costs 30% of cash on a 45% gamble for fame and brand, or you can start a foundation or hand over the keys.

media.caption: The moonshot pitch
The founders' last bet

items.title: Far fewer popups that stop the game
items.body: Pausing popups now keep about 30 seconds of play between them, or 4 game weeks at fast speeds, whichever comes first. The first card of an era and the very first popup still come at once, and paused time does not count. Launches that finish together share one results card, with up to 6 queued, and each row offers its own shortcuts. A launch result also offers to start the next version with the same team and to rerun the last campaign, so you skip the trip to Reports and Marketing. Later policy unlocks are a toast with a NEW tag on the Policies button instead of a card, and only the first policy unlock keeps its card. Fun staged moments, like the printer smash or the visitor, now hold the game clock while they play, with a Skip button on the caption. They play out at 1x and 2x, skip themselves at top speed, and hold the clock for 180 seconds at most.

items.title: Six office-movie decisions, each once a run
items.body: The banner (Consolidation, 12 or more staff): hang it for +2% output and +5% meaning drain for 26 weeks, hang it ironically for +2 team meaning with a 20% chance a visiting investor posts it sincerely (brand -1), or send it back for $300. The cover sheets: mandate them for -2% output for 26 weeks and +3 institutional knowledge, with three memos on Yak, or quietly lose the memo for +1 meaning. The red stapler, for someone with 2 or more years in: standardize for +$200 and -25 meaning for them, then 13 weeks later they find it and gain 10, or let them keep it for +5 meaning. The consultants (Consolidation, 15 or more staff), two of them called Rob: let them work for $60K, -4 team meaning, +5% output for 26 weeks and your two lowest-rated people let go, file the report for $60K, or send them home for -1 brand. The printer: take it out back for $2,500 and +6 team meaning, call the repair line for $300, or print less for -1% output for 13 weeks. And a Saturday ask: say yes for +8% output for 2 weeks at -3 team meaning and +10 strain, or refuse for +2 team meaning and -3 for the senior who asked. The printer one ends with staff carrying it out back and smashing it to a rap made for the moment.

items.title: Decisions now show up in the office
items.body: Decisions that describe something physical now put it on screen: pizza, a curtain over the moonshot, a sledgehammer, a pet carrier, letters, screens that take over, smoke, sticky notes, mug piles, moving boxes, whiteboard scrawls, a giant cheque. Staff react: they dig into the pizza, swing the hammer, peer into the carrier, sigh over a letter. Some choices leave a prop behind. Pushing through founder burnout leaves a mug bucket for 26 weeks, either hackathon sponsor leaves a giant cheque for 26 weeks, a conference booth leaves a swag box for 4 weeks, and saying not yet to the French press request leaves the French press until you buy an espresso machine. Granting an item, like the ping pong table, charges once and tells you if there is no room or no cash. A caption names what is happening, and the visitor scene now has the founders hiding from the person testing the product.

items.title: Answer Yak posts as the founder, and post yourself
items.body: Some staff posts in Yak come with two or three founder replies, each showing a small effect. They come from what is actually happening: a worn-out teammate, an incident, a launch, the rival, a late project, a full office, low cash. Only one is open at a time, and ignore it for three weeks and it counts as ignored. Six trivial decisions (the two coffee requests, the pet question, a new model dropping, a senior's side project and the app store rejection) now arrive this way instead of pausing the game, and if nobody answers, the mildest choice happens and never one that brings in an item or a pet. A Post button lets you pick from five posts. A pep talk is +2 team meaning, but -1 during an outage or when team meaning is below 30. A meme is +2, but -3 during an outage. Pizza costs $25 per person in the office for +3 meaning and +10 stamina, and counts as a backfire during an outage. Posting the same message again within 8 weeks falls flat. An announcement is +3 with a launch, hire or finished goal in the last two weeks, and -1 with no news. Asking who broke prod during an outage gives the product +3 health and costs 1 meaning, and with nothing broken it costs 2. Posts share a 2-week cooldown, and Yak can be set to All, Important or Off.

media.caption: A staff post with founder replies
Reply prompt during an incident
A quick post that backfires

items.title: Office items say who they help, and keep their front clear
items.body: Every office card now tags what the item is: the desk is a Workstation (a seat for one, and nobody can work or be hired without one), and anything with an effect for everyone is tagged Office-wide, nobody assigned. Standing Desks say so in their text and cut stamina drain by 10, 20 or 30% for the whole office by level. Items with a front zone (espresso, coffee corner, plant wall, bookshelf, library, arcade, plus the standing desk mat from level 2 and the server rack grate at level 3) now keep the tile in front of them clear, and placement refuses with Needs clear floor in front. The espresso demand no longer fires when you already have a coffee corner, and a new one fires when you have a corner and no espresso machine. Pair games at foosball and ping pong tables now happen in small offices too, so two garage founders play now and then.

items.title: You can see people grow, and the roster looks more like a real company
items.body: A promotion, an earned trait or trained skills now get a portrait toast, for example a promotion to Senior Designer with its skill gains, and clicking it opens their card. Level-ups alone stay quiet and put a yellow New pip on the staff row. Each person keeps a growth history, so the timeline on their card survives a reload, and when three or more people level up in a week the team posts a growth line in #wins. Level-ups, promotions and traits have their own sounds. Staff names now come from much wider pools, 328 first names and 265 last names, weighted toward a US tech company, with no repeats and no famous full names.

items.title: Acquisition offers come a little less often
items.body: The acquisition offer is now a little rarer in the event roll (its weight went from 6 to 4.5), still needing year 10 and the offer MRR and brand. In bot runs over 200 seeds, the balanced bot's exit rate through acquisition fell from 64.5% to 61%, back inside its target band. It is a small change to how fast a good game ends.

items.title: Policies button, tooltips, mute and clearer goals
items.body: Policies has its own bottom-bar button, and the bar is ordered by when menus usually unlock. Native browser tooltips became game-styled ones, and people and items get tooltips and a verb for what they are doing. Market trends now say what they do, and goal counts read "3 of 5 done", with a thin progress bar on count goals such as 4 of 10 staff. A mute button sits beside the speed controls. Toasts count toward the weekly limit with the most important first, and a toast that is cut off shows a more cue and opens in full on a tap. Settings gets a Camera follows big moments switch, and staged moments get a caption just above the menu bar.

items.title: Phones get a proper pass
items.body: On phones the side tray folds into a badge strip, and landscape is playable. Decision cards use the full width, New Product is one column, and toasts are smaller and out of the way. Pinch zooms the camera instead of the page, Yak tabs scroll in one row, and the build bar gets a second row so item names fit. Phones start in low graphics quality.

items.title: Music playlists per era, and new cues
items.body: Each era plays several music beds as a playlist, switching on a bar line with a crossfade after a couple of minutes. The Classic and ChatGBT loops became playlists, long Agents, Consolidation and Plateau playlists arrived, and each music-night genre alternates between two tracks. The printer, stapler, memo and banner have their own sounds, a soft ping tells you a Yak reply prompt opened, and a quick post that lands gets a small cheer while one that backfires gets a wince.

items.title: A world around the office, and eras that look different
items.body: Each stage now sits on a diorama board in its own surroundings: a suburban lot with a driveway and passing cars for the garage, a building storey above a street among towers for the Office Floor, a campus plaza for HQ. Every era also dresses the office walls with its own colour band, emblem and three signature pieces, so Agents, Consolidation and Plateau no longer look alike. Foosball tables now have a moving ball, sliding rods and goals, and new props include an incubator sign, The Box poster and pallets of oat milk.

media.caption: Agents era office
Consolidation era office
Plateau era office

items.title: Smaller fixes
items.body: Launch review quotes are distinct within a launch, fit the version, and the outlet scores average to the score the popup shows. Agent chatter no longer appears before the Agents era. Furniture drops in while paused, office moves swap in place, and people stop clipping furniture, walking through desks or covering faces with speech bubbles. Audio unlocks on more input types.

items.title: Faster checks and a trailer
items.body: Local CI got faster and safer: render checks run in parallel and skip unchanged inputs, light PRs skip the balance suite, and a main guard runs the full suite on each main commit. The scene sweep now checks for overlaps, floating props and models against their footprints. A game trailer is built by one command, and the readme links to it.

headline: Burnout, vacations and outside offers change how teams hold together, and the late game gets HQ expansion, acquisitions and mid-era decisions

items.title: Overwork, vacations, outside offers and Crunch Mode
items.body: People now wear down from overwork as well as lost meaning. Strain builds from tiredness, understaffing, crunch, being on call during an outage and covering for burnt-out colleagues. At 60 strain the game warns that someone looks exhausted, and at 85 they burn out even if they love the job. Everyone takes about two weeks off a year, staggered so at most about 15% of the team is out at once, and a crunch or an outage postpones a vacation (which adds strain). Anyone who has been around 26 weeks or more can take an outside offer, at a base rate of 2.5% a year. That rate climbs when meaning is low, when pay is under the going rate, or when someone is coasting, and drops with good perks and policies. A team with average meaning of 70 or more sends a friend with the same role and level when someone leaves. The new Crunch Mode policy gives engineers and designers 15% more output, but everyone on a project takes extra strain and meaning drain every week, so a team that lives on it burns out. The No Crunch policy does the opposite, and the Time off action sends someone away for two weeks.

items.title: Music night is a dance break, and the Waffle Party is earned
items.body: When music night comes up for the Incentives Program, the winner picks the genre: Corporate Synthwave, Motivational Polka, Aggressive Bossa Nova or Sad Lo-fi. A speaker cart rolls in, the room dims under a pulsing light in the genre's colour, and the winner dances while a few colleagues join in and others point, whisper and wave. The dance lasts as long as its track. The reward itself is unchanged: the winner gains meaning, others feel a little envy, and output gets a fading boost. The Waffle Party now sits outside the timed reward ladder, which tops out at music night and repeats. A person earns it once, by shipping their twentieth product launch or reaching the top level, and the company holds at most one every 156 weeks. Its crowd gathers on the camera side.

items.title: Late-game things to spend money on
items.body: The HQ can be expanded in three steps, each adding room for 5 more desks. The Knock-through costs $2M (rent +$6K a week) and needs 28 staff, the Roof Terrace costs $6M (rent +$8K a week) and needs 33 staff and the year 2030, and the Annex costs $15M (rent +$12K a week) and needs 38 staff and 2033. Desks are now capped at 30 on the Office Floor and the HQ base, so 45 at most, and the Office panel shows the limit. The terrace only takes outdoor items like plants, couches, the coffee corner and the ping pong table. From the Agents era, three small companies come up for sale each year, with a second round in Consolidation. Each is sized to you: its yearly revenue is 3 to 12% of yours and the price is 6 to 10 times that (20% less in Consolidation), and an offer expires after 13 weeks. Buying one needs a free desk for everyone who joins. Reports shows each offer with its price, people and payback, and a chip turns amber when it is about to expire. Two upkeep policies, Top-of-Market Pay and Office Upkeep, cost money every week to make outside offers less likely, and a Fame bar appears once you have some.

items.title: Mid-era decisions: the agent bill, a rival's mega-round, the floor next door
items.body: The long stretches between eras now have one-time decisions. 45 weeks into Agents comes the agent bill: audit every agent (8 weeks of agent spend, and rogue risk drops 30% for a year), cap the spend (automation comes down to half), or say it is fine and get an invoice 26 weeks later for 20 weeks of spend, which you can pay or dispute as a gamble. 95 weeks into Agents, with a live rival, the rival raises a mega-round. Matching their offers raises salaries 8% and halves outside offers taken for 26 weeks, reminding people why they are here adds team meaning but invites more offers, and letting them try invites half again as many. From 130 weeks into Agents, once the first HQ expansion is open and affordable, the empty floor next door offers a chance to knock through at once. In Consolidation, the first small companies for sale come with an offer to buy the best-value one. Merging with a rival now costs $150K plus $60K per point of its strength.

items.title: The AI Summit, new Saasies, the hearing and alumni
items.body: From the ChatGBT era on, a yearly decision at week 20 lets you send the company to the AI Summit, with the format rotating between a keynote demo, the "Will AI Replace Us?" panel and a hackathon. The small and big options cost $20K and $80K in the ChatGBT era, 1.5 times that in Agents, double in Consolidation and 2.5 times in Plateau. Declining twice in a row pauses invitations until you launch a new AI product. At week 50, three new Saasie categories are announced. Best AI Feature needs a live AI product scoring 8.5 or more and gives it +15 hype. Best Place to Work needs 10 or more people in good spirits, average meaning of 78 and no resignations that year, and gives +1 meaning. Most Trusted, from Consolidation, needs a year with no breach or incident and gives +2 brand. Once, from 2027 in the Agents era or later with two or more live AI products, you are summoned to a hearing: send a founder (a gamble), send the lawyers ($30,000) or decline. The committee report follows 13 weeks later, and complying early costs $40,000 but cuts customer churn for a year. People who leave become alumni, and the ending epilogue retells the run, leading with how it ended and ranking consequences above flavour.

media.caption: AI Summit hackathon decision

items.title: Meaning and Purpose
items.body: Meaning only shows from the ChatGBT era on; before that the interface shows mood and energy. About eight weeks into Agents, the company picks a mission: craft, people, trust or growth. Later decisions, like automating support, the AI-first mandate or investor headcount pressure, either keep faith with that mission or break it, and move Purpose. Purpose helps people recover and stay.

items.title: Track records, era emblems, a longer tour and cancel buttons
items.body: The staff table shows each person's role stats, such as new revenue and deals for sales, features and merged PRs for engineers, or tickets for support, with a badge for the clear leader of each stat (nothing on a tie or a team under 3 people). Each era has a round emblem on its arrival card and in the top bar. The opening tour is now seven stops with a skip button, and the first product form has a short guide to picking category, angle and size. Unfinished projects can be cancelled with a two-tap confirm. Locked office items are hidden until available, with a card announcing new ones, and dropdowns became a game-styled picker. The team chat is now called Yak.

items.title: The game gets its audio
items.body: Era music, a crowd bed, UI sounds, stingers, rare voice barks and group cheers now play, along with sounds for outages, doors, perks, pets, coffee and typing. Staff who move on, retire or get poached get a warm send-off cue, and the hire cue rises. The title screen has its own theme loop, and audio sliders are in settings.

items.title: The office talks, and characters look and move better
items.body: People now chat out loud and in Yak about what is actually going on: this week's news, the furniture that exists, the era, and a running @channel joke. Standups are varied and use each person's real work, and speech bubbles stay readable, with leader lines when lifted, and last long enough to read at 2x and 4x. Characters use hand-authored animations by default (typing, napping, burnout, walking), with simpler poses kept for Low quality. Pausing now freezes the whole office, and people walk around new furniture and get onto couches from the side.

items.title: Smaller fixes
items.body: Touch taps, targets and build mode got guardrails, and the top bar wraps and the bottom menu fits on phones. Furniture placement gives a quiet dust puff instead of confetti. Hair, hat and outfit combinations look cleaner, and the security vest no longer reads as danger red. The pause and play icons no longer vanish. Old saves get a screen explaining why, with a way to export them, and a pre-alpha notice shows the build version.

headline: The first playable company: a clock, an office that grows, and a team that talks

items.title: A company that moves up from the garage
items.body: A new company starts small and moves through three office stages, each with its own layout and screens, and the move plays out on screen instead of cutting. There is an office shop for furniture and gear, a research tree and career paths to spend effort on, and training for the staff.

items.title: Daily standups and a team chat
items.body: Teams hold a standup each day, either gathered in the office or asynchronous, and the people who speak get the daily lift. Slackk, the team chat panel, keeps a log of what everyone said, with a #standup channel and lines written for the situation. Bubbles over people's heads hold long enough to read.

items.title: A guided opening and a Needs you strip
items.body: The first game walks you through a first build and pauses while the tutorial talks. A Needs you strip lists what is waiting for your attention. Founding a company now starts with its identity, a founder pair and funding before week one. Menus pause the clock, toasts are budgeted per week and a raise shows up as a toast with its cost.

items.title: A slower clock, and a mid and late game with teeth
items.body: A week takes about five seconds, with events spread across it instead of landing all at once. Automation is real leverage now, measured against careful human play. An IPO is a real exit, and crises can reach a well-run company, so the late game has to be earned.

items.title: New art, rendered clean
items.body: The new objects and looks from this day, each on its own with a plain background. Things that come in levels show all three side by side.

media.caption: Party balloons, for the office's celebrations.
Foosball table: two people play head to head, rods spinning.
Kitchenette: the coffee corner people walk over to for a sip.
Ping pong table: a real volley, paddles picked up off the table.
Waffle station: the waffle party's buffet.
